How A 58-Year-Old Carpenter Says He Relieved His Arthritis Pain With An Ancient Copper Remedy In Only 15 Days After Being Medically Retired From His Career

The 3,000-Year-Old Therapy Big Pharma Doesn't Want You To Know About — And The Simple Band That Phil Says Changed His Days
By Joint Health Daily · Published yesterday · Updated
Phil Cleary, 58, back in his home workshop after discovering an ancient remedy that changed his life. Photo supplied.

Phil Cleary spent 34 years swinging hammers, framing walls, and building over 200 homes with his bare hands.

He wasn't just a carpenter. He was the guy neighbours called when their deck was rotting and friends trusted to help renovate their kitchens on weekends. His hands weren't just tools — they were his identity.

When arthritis crept into his fingers at 54, his doctor shrugged it off as "wear and tear." Phil pushed through it and popped ibuprofen like mints. By 57, the pain had spread to his wrists, elbows, and both knees.

He couldn't close his fist around a hammer handle — or open a jar of coffee.

Even a familiar hammer handle can become hard to hold when stiffness sets into the fingers and wrists.

At 58, Phil was medically retired. His doctor signed the papers and told him to "take it easy."

"Take it easy? I don't know how to take it easy. That's not who I am."

18 Months And Over $3,000 Spent — For Nothing

What followed was 18 months of frustration — and a small fortune poured down the drain.

  • Anti-inflammatory pills ($300+/year): 1,200mg+ of ibuprofen daily dulled the edge for a few hours, then wore off by dinner.
  • Topical creams ($500+/year): Voltaren, Tiger Balm, and Deep Heat — a tube and a half every month. "I'd rub it on at 7am. By 9am it was like I'd never put it on."
  • Glucosamine supplements (~$150): Four months of triple-strength pills with zero noticeable difference.
  • Cortisone injections (~$700 for three shots): The first lasted six weeks, the second barely three, and by the third Phil could hardly tell he'd had it — with his doctor quoting $1,500 to $2,000 a year to keep injecting multiple joints.
  • Gadgets ($160): Compression gloves ($35), a paraffin wax bath ($80), and a late-night TV copper sleeve ($45) — all used twice and stuffed in a drawer.

In 18 months, Phil spent over $3,000 on treatments that left him with a thinner wallet and a bathroom cabinet full of empty promises. Meanwhile, his world kept shrinking — no hardware store runs, no helping his son-in-law build a deck, no picking up his grandkids or building playhouses in the backyard.

A bathroom cabinet crowded with pills, creams, and supplements — the leftovers of 18 months of treatments.
"He wasn't depressed exactly. He was… disappearing. The man I married built things. This man just sat there."

Why Nothing Phil Tried Ever Worked

Here's what most arthritis sufferers never get told: those products were never designed to fix the problem. They were designed to manage it.

An anti-inflammatory pill that wears off in four hours isn't a failure — it's a business model. A cortisone shot that fades in six weeks is a subscription you never signed up for.

The entire $24 billion global arthritis industry runs on one principle: keep the customer coming back. Not because lasting relief doesn't exist — but because lasting relief isn't profitable.
